title: Image Segmentation Method Based on a Dual-Domain Coupled 2-Additive Fuzzy-Measure Capacity Network
summary: High-resolution remote sensing images exhibit large variations in object scale, ambiguous boundary transitions, and complex interactions among adjacent land-cover regions. Under sparse pixel supervision, these factors may cause object fragmentation, erroneous merging, and boundary displacement. To address these issues, a Dual-Domain Coupled 2-Additive Fuzzy Measure Network (DC2CNet) is proposed for sparse pixel-supervised remote sensing image segmentation. The proposed method extends pixel-level class prediction by jointly modeling regional consistency and boundary discrimination. A region-domain branch and a boundary-domain branch are constructed to characterize intra-region coherence and class-transition information, respectively. A dual-domain coupling mechanism is further introduced to integrate regional and boundary evidence. In addition, a 2-additive fuzzy measure decoding strategy is developed to model individual evidence contributions and pairwise evidence interactions through Möbius representation. During training, sparse pixel annotations are used to generate boundary discrimination probabilities, and neighborhood consistency constraints are introduced to optimize the boundary branch. Experimental results demonstrate that DC2CNet effectively reduces boundary ambiguity and region confusion, while maintaining accurate segmentation of small objects, elongated structures, and complex interface regions.

title: Reliability-Aware Feedback-Controlled Fusion for Spatially Disjoint HSI–LiDAR Classification
summary: This study presents a reliability-aware feedback-controlled fusion framework for hyperspectral image (HSI) and LiDAR classification under spatially disjoint conditions. Instead of committing to a fixed fusion configuration, the framework couples a library of fusion operators (geometry-aware fusion, adaptive gating, cross-modal transformer fusion and physics-informed fusion), integrated within a unified GhostConv-based architecture, with a closed-loop controller that evaluates candidate operators on validation data, accepts them only when they improve validation accuracy, and applies feedback-guided residual refinement. Experiments are conducted on Houston2013, Muufl, and Augsburg under a sample-center spatially disjoint protocol, in which training and validation samples are drawn from development blocks that are spatially disjoint from the test blocks, with seven labeled samples per class and ten random partitions. The framework achieves mean overall accuracies of 70.00%, 73.20%, and 66.34%, improving the Baseline-Ghost model on Houston2013, Muufl, and Augsburg; the improvement achieved by closed-loop training is preserved under a patch-disjoint protocol. Budget-matched analyses show that, with seven labels per class, the gain stems mainly from validation-gated closed-loop training and feedback-guided refinement, whereas the benefit of adaptive operator switching emerges as the label budget increases.

title: Sentinel-1 SAR Monitoring of River Water Surface Elevation: Effects of Wind, Waves, River Morphology and Vegetation
summary: Accurate monitoring of river water surface elevation (WSE) is important for hydrologic and flood applications, particularly where in situ observations are limited. This study evaluates Sentinel-1 Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) for estimating river WSE using a river inundation area–water surface elevation (RIA–WSE) relationship derived from high-resolution topobathymetric elevation data and investigates environmental factors affecting estimation accuracy. A total of 265 Sentinel-1 SAR images acquired during 2015–2026 covering the USGS Thebes gauging station along the Mississippi River were analyzed using six VV- and VH-based backscatter metrics, yielding 1590 WSE estimates. Comparison with a conventional 1-m digital elevation model (DEM) revealed that its representation of river water-surface elevations at the time of the elevation survey, rather than submerged channel-bed elevations, limits its applicability for estimating WSE at low river stages. Among the six metrics, log10(VV) produced the best overall performance, with an RMSE of 1.61 m, mean error of −0.96 m, R2 of 0.81, and percentage of lowest absolute error (PLE) of 44.5%. A sensitivity analysis using SAR image grid spacings of 10, 5, 2, and 1 m showed that log10(VV) maintained relatively stable estimation accuracy, whereas finer resampling did not consistently improve WSE estimates. Errors were smallest under low-flow conditions (WSE < 97.0 m), largest under medium- to high-flow conditions (97.0–102.5 m) and decreased again during flooding (WSE > 102.5 m). Analysis of 10 National Agricultural Imagery Program (NAIP) images revealed increasing vegetation along the inundation boundary above approximately 100 m WSE. Under medium- to high-flow conditions, calm conditions generally produced smaller errors than non-calm conditions, although errors did not increase monotonically with wind speed. E–W and SE–NW wind orientations generally produced larger errors than N–S and NE–SW orientations. These results indicate that WSE estimation accuracy reflects combined effects of vegetation, wind-generated water surface roughness, wind orientation, effective fetch, water depth, and river morphology. Although log10(VV) performed best overall, it provided the lowest absolute error for only 44.5% of acquisitions, highlighting the potential for condition-dependent backscatter metric selection to improve SAR-based river WSE retrieval.

title: A Complex-Valued Multiscale Feature Interaction Attention Vision Transformer for PolSAR Image Classification with Amplitude–Phase Decoupling
summary: Limited labeled data and class imbalance complicate polarimetric synthetic aperture radar (PolSAR) image classification. We propose a complex-valued multiscale feature interaction attention vision transformer (CV-MfIaViT) that combines spatial analytic-envelope preprocessing, complex-valued local feature extraction and global modeling. A two-dimensional Hilbert transform (2D HT) provides envelope features to the shallow pathway. The complex-valued amplitude–phase interaction attention (CV-APIA) module generates positive real gains through cross-modulation of pooled features; the final gating preserves the element-wise phase of non-zero input features. A complex-valued feature complementary mapper (CV-FCM), a complex-valued multiscale extractor (CV-MSE) and a complex-valued vision transformer (CV-ViT) complete the architecture. Under random-pixel sampling, the reported average accuracy (AA) exceeds CV-MsAtViT by 1.83, 3.42 and 2.48 percentage points on Flevoland, San Francisco and Nanjing, respectively. The advantage is also retained under spatial-block partitioning with shared label-free scene-level normalization. Component ablations and comparisons with two simple learned front ends characterize the combined design. The results support the evaluated architecture without isolating phase preservation as the cause of its accuracy gains.

title: Preliminary Overpass Level Assessment of Early NISAR 200 m L-Band Soil Moisture: Effects of Quality Control and Sensor Depth
summary: The NASA–ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) mission provides L-band soil moisture at 200 m, but validating its early products depends on retrieval flags, overpass collocation and sensor depth. We evaluated the beta Level-3 product against seven U.S. in situ networks (October 2025–January 2026) and the provisional product at 21 National Ecological Observatory Network sites (June–July 2026). Beta retrievals with flag 0, which averages all three candidate algorithms, were matched to in situ data within 60 min, merged by orbit and averaged over 0–10 cm sensors, yielding 261 site overpasses from 117 sites. Beta NISAR had a preliminary bias of 0.003 m3 m−3, a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.081 m3 m−3 (95% interval 0.066–0.098) and R=0.578. Accepting all flag classes increased coverage ninefold and RMSE to 0.096 m3 m−3. On common site overpasses, deeper sensors did not have significantly higher RMSE than 5 cm sensors. The exploratory provisional assessment found a wet bias of 0.110 m3 m−3, concentrated at very dry reference sites, with a pooled R of −0.038 but an anomaly R within sites of 0.259. These estimates rest on few sites and short records; validation of early NISAR products should report flag classes, overpass construction and matched depths and separate pooled from temporal agreement.

title: SNAPxtra: An Open-Source Python Workflow for Automated Multi-Temporal InSAR Deformation Monitoring with SNAP
summary: Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) is a satellite–based remote sensing technique capable of measuring surface displacement. However, InSAR measurements can be affected by temporal decorrelation, baseline geometry, and surface characteristics. Persistent scatterer (PS) and small baseline subset (SBAS) are two widely used multi-temporal InSAR techniques for addressing these limitations. Processing SAR acquisitions to derive deformation maps and displacement time series requires a series of complex steps. Many existing open-source and commercial software packages support PS or SBAS, while some support both methods, each with its own challenges and limitations. In this study, we presnet SNAPxtra, a Python-based InSAR automatic workflow to generate PS and SBAS interferometric stacks. These can be exported in the format required for time-series analysis in LiCSBAS and StaMPS. SNAPxtra has automated master selection, multi-swath and multi-frame processing, polygon-based masking, trial processing, and network generation features within an integrated workflow. The reproducibility and adaptability of SNAPxtra are demonstrated through case studies in Quetta (Pakistan), Surat (India), and Fort Worth (USA) as case studies using both PS and SBAS methods.

title: Climate and Region-Specific CO2 Effects on Wheat Phenology in Greece and Cyprus: A Satellite-Based Assessment
summary: Accurate assessment of crop phenology under changing climate conditions is essential for agricultural planning and food security, particularly in regions where wheat production is sensitive to temperature and water availability. This study examines the long-term phenological responses of wheat across six sites in Greece and five in Cyprus over a 24-year period (2001–2024), using MODIS-derived NDVI time series to extract start of season (SOS), end of season (EOS) and length of season (LOS). SOS advanced consistently in both countries, while EOS was delayed in Greece but advanced in Cyprus. As a result, LOS increased across Greek sites but showed mixed responses in Cyprus, with no significant average change. Spatial differences were associated with latitude, with higher-latitude Greek sites exhibiting later SOS and EOS, whereas temporal trends were linked to climatic variability. Linear mixed-model analyses identified temperature as the dominant climatic driver of SOS and EOS in both regions, with precipitation exerting additional, but region-specific influences. A key finding is that atmospheric CO2 emerged as an additional statistical predictor of EOS in Greece, where it was associated with later EOS, offsetting the climate-driven advance in the model, and was marginally associated with LOS extension. In contrast, no CO2 association was detected for Cyprus, possibly reflecting more constrained environmental conditions. These findings highlight the importance of integrating geographic, climatic and atmospheric variables to capture crop-specific responses and support region-specific adaptation strategies in Mediterranean agroecosystems vulnerable to climate change.

title: Radar Precipitation Uncertainty and Hydrological Applications: Mapping Topic Structure, Thematic Evolution, and Methodological Lineages Through Bibliometric and Transformer-Based Semantic Analysis
summary: Radar precipitation information with high spatial and temporal resolution is essential for flood forecasting, urban pluvial flood warning, and digital twin basins, yet radar quantitative precipitation estimation (QPE) is affected by observational errors, retrieval relationships, terrain effects, and multi-source merging. Based on 1328 Web of Science Core Collection publications (2000–2025), this study integrates bibliometric analysis, Transformer-based semantic representation, BERTopic modeling, semantic association analysis, and bibliographic coupling to map the topic structure, thematic evolution, and methodological lineages of research on radar precipitation uncertainty and hydrological applications. Nineteen micro-level topics were identified and grouped into four categories: measurement error identification and correction, uncertainty characterization and modeling, error propagation and scale effects, and operational applications and risk decision-making. The semantic structure shows that observation and correction and hydrological propagation constitute the main branches, while AI-driven forecasting is emerging. Methodological lineage analysis indicates that Statistical Fusion dominates the field, Physics provides a foundation, and AI and Hybrid methods have grown markedly in recent years, with Hybrid methods bridging physical mechanisms, statistical fusion, and data-driven approaches. Future research should integrate explainable AI, physical constraints, probabilistic modeling, and hydrological-response consistency testing to advance chain-wide uncertainty representation from observation and forecasting to hydrological propagation and risk-informed decision-making.

title: Satellite-Derived Landscape Characteristics Distinguish Streamflow Drought Occurrence
summary: The consequences of drought for rivers depend not only on the atmospheric water deficit but also on how catchments store and release water. It remains unclear how well catchment characteristics distinguish streamflow drought occurrence under similar meteorological conditions. We combined AlphaEarth satellite descriptors with principal component analysis to examine this question in 361 relatively undisturbed catchments across the conterminous United States. Using the three-month Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) and Standardized Streamflow Index (SSI), we linked meteorological droughts to subsequent streamflow droughts and assessed whether catchment landscapes helped explain differences in their occurrence, intensity and duration under comparable meteorological and initial streamflow conditions. Occurrence was most clearly associated with PC1, the dominant component of the AlphaEarth descriptors, whose landscape differences were partly reflected in drainage density and forest cover. At comparable meteorological drought durations and the same meteorological intensity and initial streamflow conditions, catchments in the upper PC1 quartile had estimated occurrence probabilities 8.1–20.9 percentage points below those in the lower quartile. The separation was greater for moderate-or-stronger drought, at 13.8–22.3 points. Higher PC1 also tended to accompany lower drought intensity, but the evidence for intensity and duration differences was less conclusive than for occurrence. These findings support the use of a common satellite-derived landscape description to identify catchments more susceptible to streamflow drought under comparable meteorological conditions, while showing that occurrence probability alone cannot indicate how severe or persistent the resulting drought will be.

title: Phenology Studies in Mediterranean Ecosystems: Assessing the Impact of Temporal and Spatial Resolution
summary: Satellite-based characterization of vegetation phenology in structurally complex Mediterranean ecosystems remains challenging because of the contrasting spatial and temporal properties of remote sensing platforms. This study evaluates how differences between sensors, including spatial and temporal resolution, influence phenological parameter extraction from NDVI time series in a cork oak woodland in central Portugal. NDVI time series from Landsat 8/9, Sentinel-2, and a ground-based spectrometer (FloX) were processed in TIMESAT to extract six phenological metrics across three vegetation types (cork oak, herbaceous vegetation, and open woodland) over three growing seasons (2022–2025). Landsat 8/9 and Sentinel-2 agreed closely for herbaceous vegetation and open woodland, whereas differences concentrated in cork oak, where Sentinel-2 estimated a start of season 161 days earlier in Year 1 and an end of season 33 to 61 days later in Years 2 and 3. Sentinel-2 retrieved higher amplitude and seasonal integral values in all vegetation types and years. Compared with FloX, satellite end of season and peak timing for cork oak were later in all years (by 72–198 and 87–203 days, respectively), whereas deviations for herbaceous vegetation were 15 days or less. These findings support multi-scale phenological characterization of Mediterranean montados and offer a baseline for future multisensor assessments of dry-land ecosystems.

title: SCALAR: Scale Anchoring and Label-Free Recalibration for Cross-Sensor Landslide Mapping Between UAV and Satellite Imagery
summary: Cross-sensor landslide mapping is limited by differences in image resolution and unreliable target pseudo-labels. We present SCALAR (Scale Anchoring and Label-Free Recalibration), an unsupervised adaptation workflow built on an exponential-moving-average teacher and ClassMix. GSD Anchoring (GSA) uses ground sampling distance metadata for bounded resampling. Logit-Otsu Calibration (LOC) jointly adjusts the pseudo-label boundary and relative retention margins. Ratio-Signed Regularization (RSR) makes these margins asymmetric according to the target-to-anchor GSD ratio. It is exploratory; GSA + LOC with symmetric margins is the recommended configuration. These modules introduce no trainable parameters. In the primary CAS region-held-out evaluation across five seeds, GSA + LOC increased the landslide intersection over union (IoU) by 17.9±4.5 points beyond scale anchoring when transferring satellite/aerial imagery (SAT) to unmanned aerial vehicle imagery (UAV), with no resolved additional gain in UAV-to-SAT. At seed 0, SAT-to-UAV threshold-independent average precision (AP) increased from 0.3484 for the anchored source to 0.4809 with GSA + LOC on held-out regions, compared with an increase from 0.6371 to 0.6495 under the original transductive protocol. Under that protocol, fixed-checkpoint region-cluster bootstrap supported GSA gains in both directions and LOC gains only in SAT-to-UAV; RSR’s 95% intervals included zero in both directions. UAV-to-SAT benefits varied across backbones, and negative transfer occurred in some tested settings. The findings support coordinating scale and pseudo-label decisions within CAS while identifying teacher reliability and target resolution as conditions to examine before broader deployment.

title: Multitemporal Analysis of Observed Flood Recurrence in an Andean–Amazonian Valley in Peru: An Integration of Field Data, SAR Images, and Cloud Computing
summary: Flood monitoring in Andean–Amazonian valleys is constrained by sparse hydrological records and persistent cloud cover. This study mapped observed flood recurrence in the Utcubamba River Valley, Peru, during 2019–2025 using Sentinel-1 imagery processed in Google Earth Engine. PRE–POST backscatter differences were classified using Otsu thresholding and spatial constraints, including a maximum slope of 5° and a 1000 m hydrographic buffer. Eight of 13 cataloged events were retained. VH thresholds had a mean ± standard deviation of −2.83 ± 0.05 dB, compared with −1.73 ± 1.11 dB for VV and −3.33 ± 1.44 dB for (VH+VV)2; the low VH dispersion is a property of the retained subset, which was selected partly on VH threshold behavior. The eight-event map covered 9842.02 ha detected as flooded at least once, with 6.29% classified as high or very high observed recurrence, concentrated near the Utcubamba–Marañón confluence. For E13, assessment against a balanced sample of 1360 reference points yielded a sample-based overall accuracy of 85.15%, flooded-class user’s accuracy of 91.64%, producer’s accuracy of 77.35%, and F1 score of 0.839. These metrics characterize the sampled sectors of E13. Agricultural classes accounted for 73.70% of the area in the 2024 land-cover overlay. Irrigation-related changes could not be fully distinguished from river flooding. The resulting count of detections across cataloged events provides complementary information for land-use planning, with interpretation bounded by temporal coverage, event selection, and reference-data availability.

title: Longitude-Resolved Spatial Organization of Quasi-Biennial-Range Stratospheric Ozone Variability from AIRS Observations
summary: Stratospheric ozone exhibits quasi-biennial-range variability, whose spatial organization can differ among pressure levels and longitudes. We analyzed Aqua Atmospheric Infrared Sounder (AIRS) Version 7 monthly ozone observations from September 2002 to December 2025 at 50, 10, and 3 hPa. A Morlet wavelet analysis of standardized anomalies characterized the 20–36-month variability, with AR(1) Monte Carlo significance tests and complementary multiple-testing and uncertainty assessments. The tropical 10 hPa band showed relatively enhanced normalized power and widespread longitudinal support: 326 of 359 eligible longitudes remained significant after a within-level Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment of band-level tests. In the global 10 hPa grid-cell analysis, 6792 of 62,191 eligible cells passed the corresponding global Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment. Conditional block-bootstrap comparisons indicated differences in some predefined longitude-sector contrasts, whereas the confidence intervals for the 10-minus-50 hPa longitude-power coefficient-of-variation difference included zero. Regressions using NOAA CPC and KIT/FU Berlin QBO wind records indicated longitude-sector heterogeneity in the 10 hPa ozone–QBO regression associations using the 50 hPa wind index. The ERA5 temperature and low-wavenumber geopotential height patterns provided meteorological context, although the assessed ozone–ERA5 spatial alignments did not pass the adopted spatial-null tests. These findings offer a pressure-dependent, longitude-resolved description of quasi-biennial-range ozone variability and selected QBO-associated statistical relationships, without establishing a unique dynamical or chemical attribution.

title: Estimation of Radio Attenuation in Radiata Pine Canopy Using Aerial Lidar and Terrestrial GNSS
summary: Data from terrestrial GNSS receivers have been combined with point clouds from aerial lidar to estimate the average attenuation coefficients of foliage in planted pine forests at GNSS frequencies. The absorption and scattering of radio signals due to the presence of vegetation can degrade signals from communications and satellite-based navigation systems, making accurate estimates of attenuation essential for predicting equipment performance. Given the potentially limited ability of lidar to penetrate dense foliage, a method was developed to estimate the average attenuation of signals based on distance travelled beneath the maximum height envelope of tree canopies. This was accomplished by using aerial lidar data to determine the outer surface of the forest canopy based on the maximum height in each horizontal bin. Each GNSS satellite detection vector was then analysed to determine the total length traversed inside of the canopy envelope. Application to regions of planted radiata pine in a managed forest outside Adelaide, South Australia, yielded average attenuation coefficient estimates for satellites with a 30–60° elevation angle of 0.36 dB m−1 for 10-year-old medium-height and 0.35 dB m−1 for 19-year-old tall trees. The demonstrated method and results provide site and vegetation-type-specific data to inform predictive models of GNSS receiver performance at specific locations.

title: Impacts of Remote-Sensing-Derived Terrain and Land-Use Datasets on Mesoscale-Model Simulations of an Extreme Heat Event over Henan, China: Sensitivity Experiments and Evaluation Against In Situ Observations and MODIS LST
summary: Remote-sensing-derived static terrain and land-cover datasets influence regional extreme heat simulations, but their effects on internal model responses and temperature performance require joint assessment. Five numerical experiments were conducted for the June 2022 Henan heatwave using five configurations drawn from three terrain datasets and four land-cover datasets. Atmospheric forcing and model physics were identical, and the inner grid spacing remained fixed at 3 km. Simulated skin temperature (TSK) was evaluated against Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer (MODIS) land-surface temperature after pixel-level spatiotemporal matching. Simulated 2 m air temperature (T2) was evaluated against observations from 111 national meteorological stations. Two diagnostic pathways examined terrain-related and land-cover-related responses. Replacing MODIS15s-lake with MCD12Q1 changed the dominant land-use category in 22.2% of Henan grid cells. Daytime sensible heat flux difference fields had spatial root-mean-square (RMS) values exceeding 20 W/m2. On the WRF Preprocessing System (WPS)-mapped 3 km grid, terrain fields derived from ASTER30 and GMTED5m had mean absolute differences of 7.5 and 22.8 m, respectively, relative to GMTED30s. Terrain-height and surface-pressure differences were strongly inversely correlated (R = −0.9990 to −0.9993), supporting hydrostatic consistency. Direct interaction residuals indicated non-additive TSK and T2 responses, and their full-period mean fields had spatial RMS values of 0.421 and 0.225 K, respectively. All configurations exhibited pooled TSK warm biases of 5.52–5.74 K, compared with an inter-configuration bias spread of approximately 0.22 K. No configuration consistently minimized temperature errors across variables and periods, and larger internal response magnitudes did not consistently correspond to smaller temperature errors. For this event and model configuration, products with higher nominal native resolution did not consistently improve temperature simulation; the independent resolution effect was not isolated. The framework combines internal diagnostics with station and satellite evaluation to assess remote-sensing-derived static inputs.

title: Applications of Deep Learning for Correcting Tropospheric Phase Delays in InSAR: A Review
summary: Tropospheric phase delay is a major error source that limits the accuracy of Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) deformation measurements, including those from the C- and X-band systems commonly examined in the studies reviewed here. Traditional correction methods, including external atmospheric models, spatiotemporal filtering, and phase–elevation empirical approaches, can partially mitigate atmospheric delays but often suffer from limited resolution, strong assumptions, or difficulties in separating atmospheric signals from complex surface deformation. Recent advances in deep learning provide new opportunities for InSAR tropospheric correction by learning nonlinear spatial and temporal relationships from interferometric observations and auxiliary information. This review provides a focused overview of deep learning-based approaches for correcting tropospheric phase delays in InSAR. Existing studies are organized according to their dominant modeling strategies, including convolutional neural network (CNN)-based spatial modeling, recurrent neural network (RNN)-based temporal modeling, generative adversarial network (GAN)-based generative learning, and other feedforward regression approaches. Key network-design strategies, training-label and dataset construction methods, and representative applications are discussed. Finally, current limitations and future research directions are discussed, emphasizing physical consistency, deformation preservation, cross-region generalization, and independent geodetic validation.

title: Ageing, Dilution and the Limits of Detection: A Canada-to-Romania Wildfire Smoke Transport Episode Observed with the RADO-Cluj ACTRIS National Facility and PACE Multi-Angle Polarimetry
summary: Smoke from the Canadian wildfires of August 2025 reached Cluj-Napoca, Romania, on 6–9 August as a thin layer at 5–8 km. We followed the plume from its source with the multi-angle polarimeters HARP2 and SPEXone and the OCI radiometer on NASA’s PACE and characterised it at the RADO-Cluj ACTRIS National Facility with a multiwavelength depolarisation lidar, a ceilometer, AERONET photometry, GRASP inversions, and HYSPLIT trajectories. Along the air mass trajectory, the HARP2 retrievals resolved the ageing of the smoke: an optical depth decaying from 0.9 to 0.2–0.3, a layer rising to 10 km and descending to 5 km, growth of the fine-mode radius, and a single-scattering albedo consistent with brown carbon loss. At the site, the lidar ratio and particle depolarisation ratio retrieved by HARP2 (52 sr, 0.042) agreed with the lidar’s derived lidar ratio and measured depolarisation (50 sr, 0.042), whereas the three satellite optical depths differed by 0.2 around an AERONET value of 0.1 and the NATALI typing networks returned three different classes. For this faint, aged plume, intensive polarimetric and vertical quantities could no longer be identified for the aerosol by its optical depth and Ångström exponent, which motivates testing an intensive-first pairing of satellite polarimetry with ground-based lidar on further episodes.

title: Noise-Robust Multiscale Structural Feature for Optical and SAR Image Matching
summary: Optical and synthetic aperture radar (SAR) image matching is fundamental to numerous remote sensing applications. Although phase congruency-based methods have been widely adopted for this task, the structural features they extract remain inherently sensitive to speckle noise, which significantly degrades matching performance. To address this limitation, we propose a novel noise-robust multiscale structural feature (NMSF) method. Unlike existing relative total variation (RTV)-based approaches that modify the RTV model or rely on phase congruency, our framework employs the standard RTV model with a principled exponential scaling scheme to construct multiscale structural maps (MSM), effectively capturing salient structural information across multiple scales while suppressing noise and mitigating modality discrepancies. Building upon the MSM, we develop an MSM-ORB detector with non-maximal suppression to extract reliable and well-distributed keypoints. We further introduce a multilayer features of oriented gradient (MFOG) descriptor with a square grid nested architecture, which fundamentally differs from the log-polar structures used in prior methods and achieves multiscale integration without dimensional inflation. Extensive experiments on publicly available datasets demonstrate that NMSF consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches, delivering superior robustness and accuracy under nonlinear intensity variations, geometric distortions, and severe speckle noise.

title: From Multi-Sensor Survey to a Multi-Scale Geospatial Digital Twin Foundation of a Historic Hill Town: Fiumefreddo Bruzio, Southern Italy
summary: Historic hill towns require geometric information capable of relating urban morphology, construction features, and structural details within a common spatial and semantic framework. This paper presents a multi-sensor, multi-scale geomatics workflow for establishing an integrated geospatial information framework for the historic centre of Fiumefreddo Bruzio in Calabria, southern Italy. A control network of 38 points provided the spatial reference for UAV and terrestrial photogrammetry, six SLAM trajectories, and 270 static laser scans covering five buildings. Point clouds generated by Structure from Motion and range-based sensors were co-registered in the RDN2008/UTM zone 33N coordinate reference system and used to produce orthophotos, digital terrain and surface models, contour lines, textured meshes, and building-scale drawings. These products were organised within an interoperable geospatial information system based on persistent links between settlement-, aggregate-, building-, façade-, space-, and macroelement-level entities. The framework also supported structural characterisation and seismic vulnerability assessment at building and urban scales, linking building screening and potential local mechanisms to their spatial interpretation. The resulting survey-based digital model supports conservation documentation, seismic screening, and street-network analysis, while providing the foundation for future digital twin development rather than an operational implementation. The study offers a transferable acquisition-to-information workflow, preserving data provenance and metric quality for risk-informed management of historic settlements.

title: MIRB-Net: Masked Inpainting and Residual Blending for Conditional SAR Target Generation on Backgrounds
summary: Enhancing the environmental generalization of Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) Automatic Target Recognition (ATR) requires diverse target–clutter combinations. Despite abundant target-free clutter, exhaustively capturing multi-background target samples is prohibitive. However, existing generative methods either distort authentic clutter statistics through full-scene reconstruction or lack autonomous generation capabilities by strictly relying on pre-existing target instances. To overcome these limitations, we propose the Masked Inpainting and Residual Blending Network (MIRB-Net) for instance-free, background-preserving, multi-class coupled generation directly onto authentic measured backgrounds. Treating the background as a measured clutter carrier, MIRB-Net synthesizes class-conditional targets in situ using three synergistic mechanisms. First, a Background-Preserving Residual Editing (BPRE) mechanism explicitly decouples spatial blending from residual prediction, effectively confining generative perturbations to the target vicinity. Second, a self-supervised Masked Inpainting Pretraining (MIP) strategy specifically designed for BPRE equips the network with crucial priors of target scattering and background statistics. Third, joint global–local adversarial supervision alongside tri-region spatial constraints ensures seamless radiometric coupling across target–clutter boundaries. Evaluated under a dedicated multidimensional assessment framework on the MSTAR dataset, MIRB-Net demonstrates superior local structural fidelity, faithful background preservation, and natural target–clutter coupling. Furthermore, hybrid data-augmentation experiments confirm that the autonomously generated samples consistently improve downstream ATR performance across diverse deep learning architectures.

title: Power Line Structure Reconstruction and Detection Method Based on Global Regression of Keypoints
summary: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) optical remote sensing provides a flexible means of mapping and inspecting power-transmission corridors. However, the automatic extraction of power lines from aerial imagery remains challenging because conductors have slender geometry, weak texture, low contrast, and discontinuous visibility and are easily affected by imaging noise, occlusion, and complex background interference. Consequently, segmentation-based methods often produce fragmented masks that limit the reliability of subsequent structural reconstruction. This study presents a power line detection and reconstruction framework based on global keypoint regression for UAV optical imagery. Rather than recursively associating adjacent keypoints, the framework regresses every keypoint belonging to the same power line toward a common start point. This shared reference is designed to avoid recursive propagation through a chain of local associations. Three complementary components are incorporated: a multi-scale region-aware feature extractor (MSRAFE) for combining local and global semantics across scales, a line feature aggregation (LFA) module for adaptive multi-level feature fusion, and a linear structure-aware feature strategy (LSAFS) for coupling local geometric cues with global structural relationships. The method was evaluated on two public aerial-image benchmarks and a self-constructed dataset. It achieved intersection-over-union (IoU) and F1 scores of 85.76% and 91.76% on PLDU and 75.23% and 83.95% on TTPLA, respectively. On the self-constructed CPLD dataset, it obtained the highest IoU (70.44%) and precision (83.87%) among the compared methods. These pixel-level results support the performance of the complete framework for detecting thin linear objects in airborne optical remote sensing imagery.

title: Integrating Multi-Source Geospatial Data and Evaluating Model Architecture for Deep Learning-Based Flood Inundation Mapping
summary: Deep-learning research on flood inundation mapping is driven largely by architectural innovation and single-run reporting. We ask whether the segmentation architecture or the input representation contributes more to accuracy in flood-event surface-water mapping. We introduce GeoHybridNet, a hybrid CNN–Transformer network, and compare it on the hand-labeled Sen1Floods11 benchmark with a U-Net, an Attention U-Net, a parameter-matched wide U-Net, and SegFormer under matched data and training. The four convolutional and hybrid models differ by at most 1.4 IoU points, and none are significantly different under event-level tests; a compact SegFormer trained from scratch is about 3.5 points lower. In factorial designs crossing three architectures with up to five input representations (five seeds each), input representation explains about 95% of the variance in water IoU and architecture about 1%. The dominant input factor is radiometric normalization: raw bands standardized per chip reach only 60% IoU and adding NDWI restores 76%, whereas the same bands standardized with training-set statistics reach 77.5% without any index. The pattern holds when permanent water is excluded. On three held-out flood events, accuracy drops by 24–26 IoU points for every model. On this benchmark, input preparation and honest evaluation matter more than architecture.

title: Benchmarking Ten Machine-Learning Algorithms for Mediterranean Forest Mapping with Sentinel-2
summary: Accurate forest-cover mapping in fragmented Mediterranean landscapes remains challenging because forests, croplands, grasslands, and sparsely vegetated surfaces often exhibit overlapping spectral responses. This study benchmarks ten supervised machine-learning classifiers for regional forest-cover mapping in the Beni Mellal-Khenifra region of Morocco, evaluates the contribution of spectral, textural, and topographic predictors, and assesses the consistency of the resulting forest map with the Hansen Global Forest Change product. A reference dataset of 2800 samples representing forest, crops/grass, bare ground, urban areas, and water was combined with an annual 2025 Sentinel-2 median composite, spectral indices, NDVI-derived gray-level co-occurrence matrix textures, and SRTM-derived elevation and slope. The samples were divided once into a stratified 70% training set and a 30% test set common to all classifiers. Redundancy, correlation (|r| > 0.80), and variance inflation factor (VIF < 10) screening, fitted on the training set only, reduced 56 candidate predictors to 16, and hyperparameters were tuned by five-fold grid-search cross-validation within the training set. On the common test set (n = 840), CatBoost, XGBoost, and the multilayer perceptron each achieved an overall accuracy of 95.95% (Cohen’s κ = 0.947), followed by Gradient Tree Boosting (95.83%); McNemar tests with Holm correction detected no significant differences among these four models. Spatial block cross-validation reduced overall accuracy by 0.3–2.7 percentage points, and CatBoost retained the highest spatially blocked accuracy (95.51% with 10 km blocks). SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) identified slope, SATVI, NDWI, and the blue band as the dominant contributors to CatBoost forest predictions. The leading maps estimated 859,057–870,663 ha of forest. CatBoost captured 90.9% of the Hansen forest extent (≥30% canopy cover) but mapped a much larger forest area; blind interpretation of stratified samples showed that 90.5% of the CatBoost-only forest was woody vegetation, mainly open woodland and matorral. These findings show that boosting ensembles combined with a compact, non-redundant predictor set provide accurate and spatially robust forest-cover maps and that differences from global products largely reflect forest definitions.

title: HRRP Target Recognition Method Assisted by Scattering Center Prior Fusion from SAR Images
summary: Accurate target prior information is an important basis for improving the detection and recognition performance of high-resolution range profiles (HRRPs). To address the insufficient reliability of prior templates in scattering-center-assisted HRRP target recognition based on SAR images, where scattering centers extracted from a single image are susceptible to noise, sidelobes, local scattering fluctuations, and variations in observation azimuth angle, this paper proposes an HRRP target recognition method based on the fusion of scattering-center priors derived from SAR images acquired at adjacent azimuth angles. Two-dimensional scattering centers at different azimuth angles are extracted by combining an adaptive point-spread function (PSF) with the two-dimensional CLEAN algorithm. Amplitude-weighted clustering is then employed to retain stable scattering structures with spatial consistency, thereby constructing a fused scattering center model. Subsequently, the fused model is projected onto the range dimension under different azimuth offsets to establish a one-dimensional scattering center prior template library. Target classification is finally performed using sliding matching based on the maximum correlation coefficient. Same-band, cross-band, and comparative experiments conducted with ground-target data sets demonstrate that the proposed method effectively improves the stability of the prior templates and target recognition performance, while exhibiting reasonable adaptability to variations in observation azimuth angle, noise level, and radar operating frequency band.

title: Volumetric Change Detection with SfM Photogrammetry from Rapid-Response Aerial Imagery After Hurricane Helene
summary: Civil Air Patrol (CAP) imagery, often the first post-disaster observation, is designed for 2D interpretation rather than multi-temporal volumetric measurement. We build post-storm digital surface and terrain models from uncontrolled CAP imagery with structure-from-motion in western North Carolina’s open Swannanoa Valley and forested Hickory Nut Gorge. Surfaces are co-registered to pre-event LiDAR using roads as pseudo ground control, corrected for terrain-correlated bias, and thresholded with a spatially variable, calibrated Level of Detection. Before bias correction, bare-earth surfaces match withheld post-event LiDAR on stable terrain to 0.68 and 0.82 m normalized median absolute deviation. Volumes are 2017-to-2024 change, lower bounds in coverage, and conditional on the bias model, residual screen, and detection window. Corrected valley surfaces record 125,000 m3 of erosion and 123,000 m3 of deposition, and a sampled image check dates about 13% of that change to the sortie. Under the same limit, the uncorrected surface reports five times the deposition, and the alternative bias model gives gross terms 3.6 to 4.2 times larger. The gorge at Chimney Rock recorded 76,000 m3 of erosion and 84,000 m3 of positive change, just under half dating to the sortie, including land deposition partly cleared before the post-event LiDAR flew. CAP-derived surfaces can capture transient storage that later surveys cannot.

title: Estimating Crown–Stem Allometry from Segmented Handheld SLAM LiDAR: Sensitivity to the Treatment of Disconnected Components
summary: Individual-tree segmentation of dense point clouds increasingly supplies the crown dimensions from which crown–stem allometry is fitted, yet no study has measured how much the fitted crown–stem exponent changes with what is done to material a segment holds but may not own. In two 1 ha plots spanning the open-to-closed canopy gradient of a Southeast Asian tropical dry forest, scanned with handheld SLAM LiDAR against a field stem map of 1320 trees, we voxelized each of 340 segments at 5 cm, split it into 26-connected components and computed crown projected area three times with identical code: on the delivered segment, after removing every component not physically continuous with the tree’s own bole (strict) and after removing only those components in which a field-mapped stem other than this tree falls inside the component’s own footprint (conservative). In the closed evergreen stand the strict treatment moved the exponent of crown area on stem diameter from 1.54 to 1.04 (paired-bootstrap difference −0.49, 95% CI −0.65 to −0.34). The conservative treatment moved it by −0.003 (−0.005 to −0.001), and its median removal was 0.000 of a segment’s points in both stands. Removal based on stem-footprint overlap therefore moves the exponent by two orders of magnitude less than removal of every disconnected component, a contrast that bounds the sensitivity without establishing the ownership of either group. The result holds with the crown base fixed at its delivered value, with the largest segments removed and on the segments whose crown base came from the primary detection rule (−0.372, −0.587 to −0.147). Its direction also holds across bole gates, crown-base thresholds, an alpha-shape crown area and connectivity voxels of 3 to 10 cm, although its magnitude scales with the voxel (−0.89 to −0.24). The crown–stem exponent obtained from segmented closed-canopy point clouds is therefore not determined by the point cloud alone, and we quantify how much of it the analyst decides.

title: Non-Negative Latent Factorization Autoencoder for Interpretable Hyperspectral Anomaly Detection
summary: Hyperspectral anomaly detection (HAD) requires effective background modeling while limiting the reconstruction of rare anomalous spectra. Conventional non-negative matrix factorization provides an interpretable endmember–abundance representation but offers limited flexibility for estimating background representations under complex spectral variability, whereas reconstruction-oriented autoencoders provide flexible nonlinear inference but often lack an explicit mixing-model structure. To bridge these two paradigms, we propose a Non-negative Latent Factorization Autoencoder (NLFA) for anomaly-oriented background modeling. NLFA employs a nonlinear encoder to estimate simplex-constrained abundance-like latent coefficients and a linear mixing model (LMM)-consistent linear decoder to represent the dominant background through endmember-like spectral bases. A column-sparse residual is jointly optimized with the latent factorization so that spectral components insufficiently explained by the learned background are retained for anomaly detection, while local spatial smoothness and endmember-diversity constraints regularize the background representation. Experiments on eight benchmark hyperspectral datasets show that NLFA achieves competitive detection performance.

title: Forest Digital Terrain Model from Copernicus GLO-30 DEM and GEDI L2A Using an Explainable Boosting Machine
summary: Accurate ground elevation beneath forest canopies is important for terrain and forest-structure analysis, yet satellite-based elevation data can be affected by canopy and terrain conditions, while spaceborne light detection and ranging (LiDAR) provides ground elevations only at discrete locations. Here, the elevation offset between the Copernicus GLO-30 DEM (CopDEM) and Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation (GEDI) L2A ground elevation was estimated using an Explainable Boosting Machine (EBM) with topographic, canopy-structure, and CopDEM-uncertainty predictors to generate continuous forest digital terrain models (DTMs) for two regions in the Republic of Korea. Validation against independent airborne LiDAR data showed root mean square errors (RMSEs) of the proposed DTM of 4.10 m in the central-western region and 3.67 m in the eastern region. In the EBM, the CopDEM height error mask (HEM), canopy cover, and aspect contributed most to the estimated offset, and the magnitude and direction of their contributions varied across canopy–terrain conditions and between regions. Residual bias increased with canopy height and became more negative on steep slopes, where RMSE also increased. These results show that the proposed approach can generate continuous forest DTMs while quantifying the contributions of the main predictors to the offset, their variation across environmental conditions, and the conditions under which residual errors increase.

title: Machine Learning Reveals Physiologically Relevant Spectral Domains for Citrus Huanglongbing Detection
summary: Huanglongbing (HLB) is the most destructive disease affecting citrus production worldwide, causing severe yield losses and tree decline. Hyperspectral proximal sensing provides detailed information on leaf reflectance; however, its effectiveness for reliable HLB detection depends on the identification of consistent and discriminative spectral patterns. In this study, hyperspectral reflectance data (400–2450 nm) were combined with supervised machine learning algorithms to distinguish HLB-positive and HLB-negative citrus samples at two complementary scales: (i) leaf-level classification using individual spectral signatures and (ii) plant-level classification based on aggregated spectral responses. Model performance was evaluated under a leave-one-field-out validation framework designed to minimize spatial dependence between training and testing data. Results demonstrated consistently high classification performance, with Logistic Regression achieving accuracies above 0.94 at the leaf level and up to 1.00 at the plant level in several configurations. Dimensionality reduction using Principal Component Analysis (PCA) preserved most of the discriminative information, although with a slight reduction in recall under certain FIELD combinations. In contrast, Class balancing produced no observed improvement, whereas hyperparameter optimization showed limited and configuration-dependent effects in classification performance. Spectral coefficient analysis revealed that the most relevant wavelengths are concentrated in the visible (400–700 nm), red-edge (700–750 nm), near-infrared (750–1300 nm), and shortwave infrared (1500–2500 nm) regions, reflecting physiological alterations associated with pigment degradation, mesophyll disruption, and changes in water and biochemical composition. Overall, hyperspectral reflectance combined with parsimonious machine learning models enabled consistent discrimination of HLB-positive and HLB-negative samples within the evaluated orchard under validation designed to reduce spatial dependence, particularly at the plant scale.

title: A Second-Order Spatial Guided Sampling Method for Outlier Removal in UAV Remote Sensing Image Registration
summary: Image registration is fundamental to UAV remote sensing data processing, but repetitive textures, viewpoint and scale variations, terrain relief, and local deformation can introduce numerous outliers into tentative correspondences. The existing random-sampling and spatial-consistency methods commonly rely on pointwise confidence or isolated pairwise relations and therefore cannot reliably determine whether a locally compatible relation receives stable group-level structural support. To address this limitation, we propose SPGSC++, a second-order spatial guided sampling method for outlier removal. SPGSC++ first uses PCA to reduce the dimensionality of tentative correspondences, thereby reducing the computational burden of subsequent spatial relation construction. It then derives second-order structural quality from the common-neighbor support of directly compatible edges and uses this quality for initial data subset selection and residual-informed data subset refinement to generate and optimize a homography. Comparative experiments show that, on the five datasets CIAP, SUIRD, UAV, ZHANGZHOU, and PAN, the proposed method achieves mean Precision, Recall, F-Score, Runtime, and mean reprojection error values of 0.9627, 0.9797, 0.9702, 0.3724 s, and 1.6454, respectively. Relative to the original SPGSC, SPGSC++ increases the mean F-Score by 0.0391 and reduces Runtime and mean reprojection error by 32.39% and 58.12%, respectively. Overall, the innovation of SPGSC++ lies in using second-order common-neighbor structural quality to guide initial subset selection and residual-informed refinement for robust estimation in UAV remote sensing image registration.

title: MoEMamba: Mixture-of-Scale-And-Attention-Experts Mamba Network for Remote Sensing Change Detection
summary: The Mamba network has recently emerged as a powerful architecture for remote sensing change detection (RSCD). Notably, the fusion of multi-scale features and heterogeneous attention mechanisms has proven effective in enhancing the performance of Mamba network. However, existing methods fail to quantitatively evaluate the actual contribution weights of different components during feature fusion, thereby limiting the interpretability of their improvements. To address this issue, this paper proposes a novel mixture-of-scale-and-attention-experts Mamba Network (MoEMamba) for the RSCD task, which has the following innovations and contributions: (1) a Siamese Mamba architecture is employed to extract features from bi-temporal images; (2) a mixture-of-scale-experts module is designed to enhance the generalization ability across multi-scale objects, which quantitatively evaluates the contribution of multiple scale-specific experts; and (3) a mixture-of-attention-experts module is proposed to improve the accuracy, which adaptively fuses complementary responses of heterogeneous attention mechanisms based on the learned weights. Extensive experiments on the WHU-CD and LEVIR-CD datasets demonstrate that MoEMamba outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. Specifically, it achieves F1 scores of 94.20% and 92.62%, and IoU values of 89.04% and 86.25%, respectively. Importantly, this study provides valuable insights into the interpretability of multi-scale feature fusion and heterogeneous attention fusion for RSCD research.

title: Multi-Class Fine-Scale Vegetation Mapping: An Automated Object-Based Workflow for New Mexico Drylands
summary: Fine-scale vegetation mapping supports habitat management, landscape change monitoring, and local planning. However, fine-scale maps that distinguish a large number of vegetation classes across broad extents remain scarce. Previous classifications using imagery with spatial resolutions of 1 m or finer have generally distinguished only six to ten classes at broad physiognomic levels and relied on training data generated exclusively through image interpretation. This study develops an object-based classification workflow to map vegetation at the Group Level of the United States National Vegetation Classification across two pilot study areas in New Mexico totaling 705,154 hectares, including the montane Jemez Mountains and the semi-arid Sevilleta region. Segmentation was performed using Geographic Object-Based Image Analysis (GEOBIA) at two hierarchical levels with 0.6 m National Agriculture Imagery Program (NAIP) imagery and a LiDAR-derived digital height model. Classification was conducted using a random forest model with 65 predictor variables derived from NAIP imagery, PlanetScope imagery, Sentinel-2 imagery, LiDAR-derived terrain surfaces, and Soil Moisture Active Passive (SMAP) soil moisture. Training and validation data were obtained from a legacy ecological plot database originally collected for purposes other than classification. Of the 34 classes initially targeted for mapping, 27 were ultimately mapped after spectrally inseparable classes were collapsed into coarser hierarchical levels. Mean overall accuracy across 1000 training and validation partitions was 54.8%, with a minimum of 51.2% to a maximum of 65.6%. Phenological variables derived from PlanetScope imagery improved overall accuracy by an average of 6.5 percentage points. Overall classification accuracy varied by 12.7 percentage points across partitions, indicating that overall accuracy estimates based on a single training and validation split may provide a poor representation of expected model performance.

title: A Controlled Intercomparison of Altimeter Wet Tropospheric Correction Retrieval Algorithms Using Sentinel-6MF Observations
summary: A key correction in altimetry measurements is the wet tropospheric correction (WTC), which accounts for the delay on the measured range predominantly caused by water vapor in the troposphere. The WTC is currently one of the main sources of error affecting the altimeter range over ocean surfaces, with direct impact on estimates of sea surface height and the global mean sea level. Most current altimetry missions rely on onboard passive microwave radiometers that measure the brightness temperature at key frequencies for the spatio-temporal collocated estimation of the WTC. For such missions, the current operational algorithms for the estimation of the WTC can be placed in two categories: those using a neural network and those using a log-linear equation dependent on classes of WTC and windspeed. These two methodologies both follow a semi-empirical approach, but differ significantly in the inputs used, the training databases on which they are developed, and the mathematical approach itself. The objective of this study is to conduct a comprehensive comparison between these two algorithms, focusing solely on the mathematical aspect, in order to determine if the differences in the approaches of the two algorithms have a significant effect on the resulting WTC products, their performance and their limitations. To ensure the identical conditions required to achieve this, we develop the two algorithms so that they take the same inputs, have the same training database, and then we apply them to identical simulated and observed datasets to determine their performance. We use the three-frequency configuration (18.7 GHz−23.8 GHz−34 GHz) of the Advanced Microwave Radiometer for Climate (AMR-C) on Copernicus Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich (Sentinel-6MF), and radiative transfer modelling using the Radiative Transfer for TOVS (RTTOV), to create a simulated database that will serve for both development of the algorithms and performance evaluation. Both algorithms are then applied to the same observations from Copernicus Sentinel-6MF to characterise their observational performance in comparison to both model and operational products, as well as to each other. We find that, despite the significant differences in the two methodologies, when the algorithms are developed and applied to the same databases, they deliver very similar performances both on simulated and observed datasets and face similar limitations. In addition, for both algorithms we find performances similar to or slightly better than that of the operational WTC product for Copernicus Sentinel-6MF.

title: A Spatio-Temporal Fusion Method for Mine Subsidence Based on Decoupling the Basic Deformation Field from Residuals Using InSAR-GNSS
summary: Ground surface subsidence resulting from underground mining is characterized by significant spatial deformation gradients and nonlinear temporal deformation. A single monitoring technique is insufficient to simultaneously achieve extensive spatial coverage and high temporal continuity. Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) provides high spatial resolution but is limited by sparse temporal sampling, whereas the Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) offers dense temporal sampling but with restricted spatial coverage. To address these limitations, this study introduces a spatio-temporal fusion method combining InSAR and GNSS, based on baseline deformation field–residual decoupling (BR-STKF), specifically applied to the Banji Coal Mine in the Huainan Mining Area, Anhui Province. Sentinel-1 SBAS-InSAR is employed to derive Line-Of-Sight (LOS) deformation time series, while three-dimensional GNSS displacements are projected onto the LOS direction. A daily scale baseline deformation field is constructed using pixel-wise Kalman filtering and Rauch–Tung–Striebel (RTS) smoothing. Subsequently, residual signals between the InSAR/GNSS observations and the baseline field are estimated utilizing a correlation-anchored multiscale spatial basis and an information-form Kalman filter. Helmert variance component estimation is introduced to adaptively adjust the weights of InSAR and GNSS observations. To demonstrate the reliability of the proposed framework, a quantitative validation was conducted. The experimental results yielded root mean square error (RMSE) values of 6.37 mm for strict spatial leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) and 2.84 mm for retrospective reconstruction with missing InSAR phases. These results are competitive and comparable to leading benchmarks such as the Spatio-Temporal Kalman Filter (STKF), while achieving lower mean RMSEs than baseline methods such as Spatio-Temporal Random Effects (STREs), Enhanced Spatio-Temporal Random Effects (eSTREs), Improved Spatio-Temporal Random Effects (ISTREs), Multi-resolution Orthogonal Polynomial Basis (MOP), and ST-Kriging. However, the statistical stability of differences among models requires further verification with additional independent data. The findings suggest that the baseline deformation field–residual decoupling strategy effectively integrates the spatial coverage of InSAR with daily GNSS observations, offering a viable framework for daily scale line-of-sight (LOS) deformation reconstruction in mining areas.

title: Contrasting Vegetation Productivity Responses to Four Compound Temperature and Soil Moisture Extremes Across China
summary: Compound temperature and soil moisture extremes threaten terrestrial carbon uptake, but their contrasting ecological impacts remain poorly understood. We assessed dry–hot (DH), wet–hot (WH), dry–cold (DC), and wet–cold (WC) events across China from 2001 to 2025. The analyses combined daily air temperature, root-zone soil moisture, and MODIS-derived gross primary productivity (GPP). We quantified event occurrence, negative-response probability, cumulative GPP loss, and recovery time, and examined environmental predictors using explainable machine learning. WC events were most frequent, whereas DH events lasted longest. WH frequency increased over the study period, while DC frequency declined. DH and DC produced negative GPP responses in 63.5% and 67.1% of classifiable events, respectively. Among negative-response events, DH had the largest national mean cumulative event-period GPP loss below the −0.5 SD threshold (2.85 g C m−2) and the longest conditional recovery time (3.17 days). WC losses exceeded DC losses despite a lower negative-response probability. Losses varied with elevation, season, and event severity. Vapor pressure deficit dominated predictions of DH negative responses and losses, whereas other event types showed greater contributions from radiation, precipitation, and soil texture. These findings highlight the need to distinguish event occurrence, response probability, productivity loss, and recovery when assessing ecological risks from compound extremes.

title: Improved Forest Parameter Estimation Using Registered Airborne–Terrestrial Point Clouds via a Novel Adaptive Clustering and Vertical Layering Method
summary: Diameter at breast height (DBH) and tree height are core parameters for forest monitoring. LiDAR enables rapid high-precision point cloud acquisition, yet single-platform data have limitations: airborne laser scanning (ALS) cannot capture sub-canopy structure, while terrestrial laser scanning (TLS) cannot fully acquire canopy information. Based on 92 plots in Guangxi, this study proposes a weighted point-to-normal iterative closest point (WPN-ICP) registration algorithm for high-precision fusion of ALS and TLS point clouds, with comparisons to trimmed iterative closest point (TrICP) and iterative closest point (ICP). An adaptive density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise (DBSCAN) algorithm was developed for diameter at breast height (DBH) estimation, and a DBH cluster-based vertical layering method (DCVL-THE) for tree height estimation. Three segmentation-based methods—canopy height model (CHM), region growing (RG), and comparative shortest path (CSP)—were selected for comparison. WPN-ICP achieved a mean MAE of 0.0359 m, with reductions of 85.87%, 69.03%, and 73.00% compared with coarse registration, TrICP, and ICP. Using the fused point cloud, DBH estimation achieved an RMSE of 0.6326 cm with an RRMSE of 5.18%, and tree height estimation achieved an RMSE of 0.7160 m with an RRMSE of 6.58%. Compared with the suboptimal CSP method, the RMSE and RRMSE for DBH were reduced by 41.79% and 41.68%, and for tree height by 25.66% and 25.68%. This method does not require full individual-tree or crown segmentation, thereby avoiding the error propagation associated with such segmentation and enabling accurate stand-scale estimation.

title: ECSA-UNet: End-to-End Compressive Spatial-Spectral Attention UNet for Hyperspectral Image Classification
summary: Hyperspectral image (HSI) classification is a fundamental remote sensing task, but the high-dimensional nature of HSI data poses challenges for acquisition, storage, transmission, and processing. To mitigate these issues, researchers have developed compressive classification methods based on the coded aperture snapshot spectral imaging (CASSI) system, enabling direct classification in the compressed domain without reconstructing the full hyperspectral cube. However, existing methods often fail to fully leverage spatial-spectral correlations, suffer from limited multi-scale feature extraction, and are constrained by fixed receptive fields and degradation caused by compression. To overcome these limitations, we propose ECSA-UNet, an end-to-end framework that directly classifies compressive spectral measurements from CASSI. The model introduces a spatial-spectral decoupling module and refines the U-Net architecture with global–local feature extraction, Spatial-Spectral Attention, a Multi-Scale Enhancement Pyramid and Cross-Stage Connections, enabling dynamic receptive fields, improved long-range dependency modeling, and robust local–global feature fusion. Moreover, the CASSI coded aperture is parameterized as a trainable component, allowing for joint optimization of coding and classification within an end-to-end learning paradigm. Extensive experiments on four benchmarks show ECSA-UNet achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, and ablations confirm each module’s contribution. In addition, it maintains an effective trade-off between parameter overhead and computational efficiency, offering a viable solution for latency-sensitive hyperspectral remote sensing tasks.

title: A Scanline Keypoint Constraint-Based Method for Correcting Scale-like Errors in UAV-ALB
summary: To address scale-like errors in local point clouds caused by pitch angle errors in unmanned aerial vehicle-borne LiDAR bathymetry (UAV-ALB) systems, this study proposes a correction method based on scanline keypoint constraints. First, the point cloud is traversed using scanline information to extract geometric keypoint features from each scanline. Next, a scale-like error correction model is constructed based on the distance differences between keypoints at the start and end of overlapping scanlines, and the pitch angle correction value is estimated using a forward–backward fusion approach. The estimated correction is then applied to the attitude data, and the point cloud is reprocessed. This procedure is iterated until the convergence criterion is satisfied. Experimental results show that, after correction, the horizontal root mean square errors (RMSE) of the two datasets decrease from 0.217 and 0.283 m to 0.025 and 0.030 m, respectively, while the elevation RMSE values decrease from 0.227 and 0.241 m to 0.006 and 0.004 m, respectively. These results demonstrate that the proposed method effectively mitigates scale-like errors in UAV-ALB point clouds and substantially improves their geometric consistency and elevation accuracy.

title: Adaptive Stratified Screening and Weakly Supervised UNet with Sparse ALS Refinement for Forest Canopy Height Mapping
summary: Forest canopy height is a key parameter for estimating forest biomass and carbon stocks, as well as a fundamental indicator for assessing forest ecosystem health. Although existing 10 m resolution global canopy height products are free and open-source, they suffer from substantial systematic errors due to the inherent biases of spaceborne LiDAR and the nonlinear relationship between optical imagery and canopy height, making them insufficiently accurate as direct training labels for deep learning. This study proposes a complete framework of “adaptive stratified screening, followed by weakly supervised UNet training and minimal ALS post-processing refinement.” First, using the 12 spectral bands of Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery, the OOB distance is calculated via weighted random forest as an anomaly metric. Through systematic comparison of three anomaly metrics (Cook’s distance, OOB distance, and standardized residuals) and five retention ratios (30–50%), the OOB distance at 40% retention is identified as optimal. An adaptive retention strategy based on tree height stratification is then implemented: for low-tree areas (<20 m), 40% of low-anomaly samples are uniformly retained; for tall-tree areas (≥20 m), the retention ratio is dynamically adjusted according to the proportion of tall-tree pixels (95% when tall-tree proportion < 10%, 70% when 10–30%, and 50% when ≥30%). The screened high-confidence Lang data are then used as supervisory signals to train a UNet model for predicting canopy height across the entire region, producing an initial canopy height map (MAE = 6.97 m, Bias = +4.21 m). Finally, using only a minimal amount of airborne LiDAR data (down to 0.1% area proportion), with a 14-dimensional input comprising the initial predicted height, screening mask values, and the 12 spectral bands of Sentinel-2, a multilayer perceptron is independently trained for each region to perform post-processing refinement of the initial predictions. Experiments based on 68 independent regions from the Open-Canopy dataset, with a strict regional split (34 validation/34 test), show that post-processing refinement reduces the test set MAE from 6.97 m (ASS) to 3.29 m (0.1% ALS, a 52.8% improvement, 58.1% improvement over the original Lang product), Bias from +4.21 m to −0.13 m, and RMSE from 8.95 m to 4.72 m. Even when the ALS proportion is reduced to 0.01%, the MAE remains 3.57 m (a 48.8% improvement). Statistical significance testing (paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n = 34) indicates that ASS+MLP(0.1%) significantly outperforms ASS (p < 0.00001). This study provides an effective technical pathway for regional refinement of global canopy height products.

title: Consistency of HY-2B/C/D Altimeter Sea State Products in Chinese Coastal Seas: Wave Height, Wind Speed, and Parameter-Dependent Inter-Satellite Bias
summary: The HY-2B/C/D constellation delivers routine altimeter significant wave height (SWH) and sea-surface wind speed over the Chinese coastal seas through four product streams (GDR, IDR, ODR, and SDR), yet whether the three satellites are mutually consistent, and whether that consistency is the same for both parameters, has not been established. We assess three years (2023–2025) of 1 Hz Ku-band retrievals against 30 quality-controlled coastal buoys, using a deduplicated matchup database, a common-buoy and common-period protocol with bootstrap confidence intervals, and triple collocation against ERA5. Within each satellite, the product streams are consistent for both parameters: the reprocessed GDR shifts the operational SWH by a sea-state-independent −0.157 m and the wind streams coincide to rounding. Across satellites, consistency is parameter-dependent. For SWH, the biases on common buoys span 0.18 m; HY-2B has the lowest random error, significantly lower than HY-2D, and HY-2C cannot be separated from either in random error. For wind speed, HY-2C reads about 1 m s−1 low in all four Chinese seas and in every wind band once the bands are defined by an independent reference, so that most of the offset is removable by a constant. The near-shore degradation of SWH inside 50 km largely reflects the sub-0.5 m sea states that dominate the near-shore buoys, and wind speed shows no comparable coastal signal. We translate these findings into applicability bounds and a parameter-aware recipe for merging the constellation.

title: TP-YOLO: Thermal-Prior-Enhanced Photovoltaic Anomaly Detection in UAV Thermal Infrared Imagery
summary: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) thermal infrared remote sensing can rapidly acquire thermal-response information for large-scale photovoltaic (PV) arrays. Nevertheless, local thermal anomalies occupy small regions within aerial images; their features tend to degrade during successive down-sampling. Moreover, model deployment on edge devices is constrained by limited computational and memory resources. To address these challenges, this paper proposes TP-YOLO, a photovoltaic anomaly-detection approach, and implements it on the Zynq-7020 hardware platform. First, a three-channel thermal-prior input consisting of luminance distribution, local luminance difference, and a luminance gradient is constructed from pseudo-color infrared images, and explicitly characterizes thermal anomalies without requiring absolute-temperature measurements. Next, the detection scales of YOLOv11n are adjusted to P2/P3/P4. Modules including A-C3k2, Conv + Add, and TLCB are adopted to optimize feature extraction and multi-scale fusion, preserving local anomaly features while restraining model complexity. On the hardware side, a PS/PL co-processing architecture is employed. A dedicated convolution IP, ADD IP, and Window IP are designed for convolution, element-wise fusion, and local-window operations, respectively. INT8 quantization and ping-pong buffering are further utilized to realize network deployment. On the PV HSD test set, TP-YOLO achieves an mAP@0.5 of 77.5% and an mAP@0.5:0.95 of 33.7%, with 1.91 M parameters and 6.2 GFLOPs computational cost. In cross-dataset evaluation on the Drone Dataset without fine-tuning, the mAP@0.5 reaches 64.4%. After deploying the INT8 quantized model onto Zynq-7020, the implemented system yields an mAP@0.5 of 76.8%, achieving single-frame inference latency of 162 ms and throughput of 6.17 FPS at 150 MHz, with a power consumption of 3.4 W.

title: Annual National Land Cover Database Collection 1.0: 39-year record of land cover and land cover change products across the conterminous U.S.
summary: To meet the growing need for timely, frequent, and consistent long-term land surface information, the Annual NLCD Collection 1.0 integrates methodologies from the National Land Cover Database (NLCD) and the Land Change Monitoring, Assessment, and Projection (LCMAP) initiative with modern geospatial deep-learning approaches. The resulting product suite provides six annual 30-m products for the conterminous United States (CONUS) spanning 1985–2023: Land Cover, Land Cover Change, Land Cover Confidence, Fractional Impervious Surface, Impervious Descriptor, and Spectral Change Day of Year. The overall accuracy of the NLCD 16-class thematic land cover product was 64.7 ± 0.5% across the study period and increased to 76.9 ± 0.4% when agreement included a match with either the primary or alternate reference label. Overall accuracy remained stable over time ranging from 64.5% to 65.0%. Even with increased temporal resolution, Annual NLCD maintained comparable accuracy to that of previous NLCD products mapped at 2–3-year intervals. Change detection accuracy for Annual NLCD was low, consistent with the difficulty of detecting and dating annual land cover transitions. User's and producer's accuracies varied considerably across change themes. Water gain and loss, forest loss, and shrubland gain were the better-detected change types, while most other change themes had accuracy <40% when allowing a ± 2-year buffer to define agreement. Despite its finer thematic classification scheme, the Annual NLCD product substantially improved change accuracy relative to LCMAP. Based on the Annual NLCD maps, approximately 19.4% of CONUS experienced at least one land cover change during 1985–2023. Annual NLCD products provide a consistent annual record of land cover and land use information to support diverse downstream applications.
