title: Advancing remote sensing of carbon fractions in coastal waters: retrieval algorithms and optical proxies for Sentinel-2 MSI and Sentinel-3 OLCI
summary: A thorough understanding of the global carbon pools and cycle is essential for understanding and predicting the effects of climate change. Coastal waters play a key role in the global carbon cycle but remain poorly understood due to their optical complexity, high spatial variability, and sensitivity to climate change. Satellite remote sensing data can provide high spatial and temporal resolution for carbon monitoring at local, regional, and global scales. This study estimates the potential of Sentinel-2 MSI (S2) and Sentinel-3 OLCI (S3) for mapping carbon fractions in coastal waters. In situ hyperspectral reflectance measurements and concentrations of different carbon fractions, namely Total Organic Carbon (TOC), Dissolved Organic Carbon (DOC), Particulate Organic Carbon (POC), and Dissolved Inorganic Carbon (DIC), were used. Bio-optical and physical water parameters, as well as carbon fractions, were measured in the coastal areas of the eastern Baltic Sea from 2023 to 2024. In situ reflectance spectra were recalculated to S2 and S3 band reflectance using their respective spectral response functions. Regression models, including linear regression and machine learning methods, were developed and validated against in situ data to estimate carbon fractions. For S2, the combinations of green and red or red-edge bands achieved the best performance in carbon retrieval, with R 2 values of 0.67, 0.64, and 0.56 for TOC, DOC, and DIC, respectively. The corresponding MAPE values ranged from 14% to 18%, and biases were close to zero. Slightly higher accuracies were obtained with S3 simulations. The S3 models that used reflectance at 490, 620, and 665 nm produced the most accurate estimates for both TOC ( R 2 = 0.71) and DOC ( R 2 = 0.67). For DIC, the best predictive model combined information from 510, 665, and 709 nm bands, achieving R 2 of 0.62. Among the tested optical proxies, CDOM absorption at 443 nm showed the most consistent relationship with TOC, DOC, and DIC ( R 2 = 0.56–0.30). The study represents a significant step forward in the remote sensing of coastal waters, and if adopted, the proposed carbon-fraction products could enable substantial progress across various fields, from carbon-cycle research to monitoring and policymaking.

title: Uncertainty as the key to interoperability: Traceable frameworks for space-based imaging spectroscopy
summary: By the end of this decade, several space agencies and commercial operators will develop and launch the next generation of space-based Earth observation satellites. This paper focuses on imaging spectroradiometers, which measure solar radiation reflected by the Earth’s surface across the ultra-violet, visible and short-wave infrared spectral ranges using hyperspectral sensors. To enable interoperable use of datasets from this growing constellation of sensors, it is essential to understand and manage differences between the measurements of the same target under similar conditions. These differences arise from multiple factors: real variations due to instrument design (e.g., differing spectral responses or viewing geometries), differences in Level 1 processing approaches based on pre-flight and post-launch calibration strategies, differences in higher-level processing into biophysical quantities, and any residual biases between sensors caused by measurement or processing errors — some of which may not be fully captured in reported uncertainties. A consistent approach to the analysis and documentation of uncertainties supports intercomparison between datasets. By assessing whether measurements agree within the expected uncertainty associated with the comparison, or identifying and quantifying systematic deviations when they do not, it becomes possible to validate interoperability and diagnose discrepancies. This paper outlines key concepts for harmonising uncertainty analysis and reporting techniques across missions, including the use of structured uncertainty propagation frameworks such as uncertainty trees. The goal is to initiate a roadmap for understanding and quantifying uncertainties in a way that facilitates robust intercomparison of multiple space-based imaging spectroradiometer measurements.

title: PACE hyperspectral observations enable a new paradigm for global mapping of terrestrial gross primary production
summary: Accurate quantification of terrestrial gross primary production (GPP) is fundamental to understanding plant productivity, ecosystem function, and carbon-climate feedbacks. Existing approaches typically rely on meteorological, soil, and other ancillary inputs, which introduce substantial uncertainties at regional to global scales. NASA's Plankton, Aerosol, Cloud, ocean Ecosystem (PACE) mission, carrying the Ocean Color Instrument (OCI), provides the first contiguous global hyperspectral observations from space. Using 122 spectral bands from PACE, we developed a data-driven framework based on partial least squares regression to generate an 8-day global GPP product. The model achieves a robust performance (R 2 = 0.71, RMSE = 1.93 gC m −2 d −1 ), comparable to models that incorporate meteorological drivers, and outperforms approaches based on broadband reflectance or vegetation indices. PACE-derived GPP showed broad spatial correspondence with solar-induced fluorescence (SIF), including hotspots across high productivity regions such as the U.S. Corn Belt, the Amazon and Congo basins, and the Indo-Gangetic and North China Plains. This strong spatial coherence supports the physiological relevance of the PACE retrievals. Our results demonstrate that hyperspectral observations provide a direct, observation-driven framework for estimating plant productivity at the global scale, opening new opportunities for monitoring vegetation responses to environmental change.

title: Dem-assisted visual geolocation integrating ephemeris-based orientation correction with Multi-Scale skyline features
summary: Accurate geolocation in GNSS-denied mountainous environments remains a significant challenge for navigation and field operations. While vision-based methods using terrain features like skylines offer a promising passive solution, their performance is often hindered by unknown camera orientation, low feature discriminability across vast areas, and severe degradation under nighttime conditions. To address these limitations, this paper presents a novel visual geolocation framework that synergistically couples ephemeris-based orientation correction with multi-scale skyline feature matching. First, an Edge-Enhanced SegFormer-B3 (EESFormer-B3) network is developed for robust skyline extraction from query images, where a lightweight Edge Gate mechanism is integrated to refine boundary precision, particularly under low-light scenarios. Second, we propose a camera heading estimation method utilizing solar and lunar ephemeris, eliminating reliance on external heading sensors and drastically reducing the matching search space. Third, for matching, a hierarchical composite feature is designed, encoding the skyline's global shape trends, local directional variations, and dominant structural distributions to ensure robustness against repetitive terrain patterns. Extensive experiments were conducted in a complex 700 km² mountainous region. The results demonstrate that our method achieves a localization success rate of 82% (daytime) and 76% (nighttime) within a 250-meter error threshold. The ephemeris-based correction alone accelerates the matching process by over 30 times compared to an unconstrained orientation search. This work provides a reliable, efficient, and illumination-invariant geolocation solution, with strong potential for applications in autonomous navigation, search and rescue, and other field missions in GNSS-compromised natural environments.

title: The Bovine Slurry Index (BSI): An integrated framework for manure pond mapping using GeoFM-derived cattle-operation detection and Sentinel-2 spectral formulation
summary: Quantifying greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions from livestock operations is a prerequisite for reconciling bottom-up inventories with atmospheric observations. However, global GHG reporting remains limited by a lack of spatially explicit data on animal waste management systems (AWMS), forcing reliance on coarse regional assumptions rather than operation-level observations. Existing geospatial foundation models partly address this spatial gap by mapping cattle-operation footprints that provide upstream spatial context, but contextual detection alone cannot identify the manure-management features within them. To address this gap, we introduce the Bovine Slurry Index (BSI), an empirical Sentinel-2 spectral index for detecting liquid/slurry manure ponds within known cattle-operation footprints. The primary formulation, BSI-E, uses calibrated narrow-NIR (B8A) and SWIR-1 (B11) reflectance bounds derived from manure pond samples in the United States and China. The index targets the empirically observed intermediate NIR-SWIR response of manure ponds relative to clear water, vegetation, dry holding pens, and exposed soil. Calibration used 2,730 pond samples from the U.S. and China, and segmentation was evaluated against 945 reference polygons across all five geographic regions. BSI-E produced stronger pond-to-background contrast and higher segmentation accuracy than evaluated water indices, with dataset-level intersection-over-union (IoU) ranging from 0.26 in Brazil to 0.68 in the United States and precision reaching 0.91. Optimal thresholds varied geographically from 0.25 to 1.00, and performance was strongest in dryland feedlot systems and lower in humid or spectrally mixed settings. BSI provides a target-specific spectral method for generating operation-scale evidence that could inform AWMS activity data within these footprints.

title: High spatial resolution Greenland Ice Sheet mass change linked to Greenland Blocking and North Atlantic Oscillation
summary: The low spatial resolution (300–400 km) of Gravity Recovery and Climate Experience (GRACE) and the 11-month data gap between GRACE and GRACE Follow-On (GRACE-FO) complicate the evaluation of long-term ice mass loss at sub-region scale. Although several studies have downscaled GRACE data for water storage evaluation, efforts to downscale ice mass change are limited. Here, we utilized multiscale geographically-weighted regression (MGWR) to improve the spatial resolution of GRACE-derived ice mass change from 0.25° to 5 km in Greenland Ice Sheet (GrIS). The reconstructed results after downscaling demonstrate consistent temporal variation and reduced noise compared to other reconstruction methods for sub-regions and the entire GrIS. They can capture finer signals of ice mass change while maintaining original spatial characteristics. Validation against free air gravity anomalies changes also demonstrates the superior performance of the downscaled results over the reconstructed CSR Mascon data. For overlapping lines, the mean correlation coefficient (CC) increases from 0.13 to 0.32, with the mean root mean square error (RMSE) decreasing from 1.36 to 1.13. At the intersection points, the mean CC improves from 0.06 to 0.30, and the mean RMSE is reduced from 1.33 to 1.05. They are further used to detect the contributions of Greenland Blocking (GB) and North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) to high-resolution ice mass change through precipitation and runoff in four sub-periods, during which the driving factors affecting ice mass change differ significantly. Additionally, NAO and GB can influence ice mass change through solid ice discharge by impacting surface temperature and sea-ice concentration.

title: From pixel-level retrievals to bay-scale nutrient dynamics in Pärnu Bay using Sentinel-3 OLCI
summary: Monitoring nutrient dynamics is essential for assessing eutrophication in coastal waters, yet conventional in situ observations provide limited spatial coverage. This study evaluated the capability of Sentinel-3 Ocean and Land Colour Instrument (OLCI)-derived nutrient products to represent seasonal and interannual dynamics of total nitrogen (TN) and total phosphorus (TP) in Pärnu Bay, Gulf of Riga, during 2016–2024. Nutrient concentrations were estimated using regionally adapted OLCI retrieval algorithms and compared with in situ observations at pixel, seasonal, and annual scales. An additional comparison with operational Copernicus Marine Environment Monitoring Service (CMEMS) nutrient modelling products was carried out. Pixel-level validation yielded moderate agreement between OLCI-derived and in situ observations (TN: R 2 = 0.50, NRMSE = 26.5%; TP: R 2 = 0.33, NRMSE = 30.9%). Independent temporal validation using 2022–2024 observations retained comparable agreement (TN: R 2 = 0.44 and TP: R 2 = 0.47). However, spatial and temporal aggregation resulted in stronger overall correspondence and substantially lower error metrics. Seasonal TN products achieved an R 2 of 0.75 and NRMSE of 14.7%, while annual products reached an R 2 of 0.68 and NRMSE of 8.6%. Similar improvements were observed for TP, where annual aggregation increased R 2 to 0.54 and reduced NRMSE to 10.0%. The OLCI-derived products captured seasonal nutrient variability, interannual nutrient tendencies, and spatial nutrient gradients associated with riverine influence. These findings demonstrate that moderate pixel-level retrieval accuracy does not necessarily limit bay-scale monitoring capability. Spatially and temporally aggregated Sentinel-3 OLCI products provide a valuable complement to conventional monitoring programmes and show considerable potential for long-term eutrophication assessment in optically complex Baltic coastal waters.

title: Satellite observations reveal expanding high-latitude warming hotspots and regional contrasts on global surface temperature change
summary: Understanding the spatial and temporal variability of global surface warming is important for anticipating regional climate extremes and potential tipping points. However, conventional temperature indicators based on spatial averaging may obscure the evolution of persistent warming hotspots and the regional processes associated with surface temperature changes. Here, we analyze satellite-derived global land–ocean surface temperature (GLST) data from 2003 to 2023 and propose a three-dimensional (latitude-longitude-time) spatiotemporal clustering framework to characterize global warming patterns and identify persistent heat clusters. Globally, GLST increased at a rate of 0.025 ± 0.007 K/y, with land warming occurring 60% faster (0.034 ± 0.012 K/y) than over oceans (0.021 ± 0.006 K/y). Warming peaked prominently at ∼ 45°N (0.075 K/y in the Western Pacific; 0.066 K/y over Europe), primarily driven by dynamics in snow-climate zones and boreal forests. Spatiotemporal clustering revealed expanding heat anomalies in northern high latitudes (>45°N), where intensity (+0.027 K/y) and spatial coverage (+0.322 × 10⁶ km 2 /y) were positive; both metrics were larger in 2013–2023 than in 2003–2012, although the short-term trend is sensitive to individual extreme years. Notably, over land, non-radiative factors, including latent heat flux and soil moisture, were associated with regional differences in surface warming, with evaporative cooling effects reducing warming in several moisture-limited regions. These findings highlight the value of satellite observations and spatiotemporal clustering for identifying global warming hotspots and developing targeted adaptation strategies.

title: Assessing forest structural dynamics and post-disturbance early-stage recovery using PlanetScope imagery and photogrammetric point clouds
summary: Forests in the southeastern United States (US) are frequently disturbed by wind events, such as hurricanes, tornadoes, and severe windstorms, affecting ecosystem resilience, biodiversity, and carbon storage. Monitoring post-disturbance forest changes is challenging due to the limited availability of spatially continuous and temporally high-resolution canopy height data. To address these limitations, we evaluated the potential of PlanetScope data to assess forest structure and thematic changes across three wind-affected sites in the southeastern US: Oakmulgee (tornado), Flagg Mountain (straight-line wind), and Weeks Bay (hurricane). We used multi-stereo PlanetScope imagery to generate photogrammetric point clouds, which were processed to extract a suite of discrete canopy height metrics at different spatial resolutions (3 m, 10 m, 15 m, and 20 m) and validated using airborne lidar-derived canopy height metrics. Random Forest (RF) regression models were then developed using PlanetScope imagery, acquired concurrently with airborne lidar across study sites, and the trained models were applied to produce pre- and post-disturbance canopy height maps. Similarly, RF classification models were developed for three scenarios (airborne lidar acquisition date, pre-wind, and post-wind), and applied to generate forest/non-forest maps for pre- and post-disturbance periods, enabling assessment of thematic changes following wind disturbance. Results indicate that upper canopy height percentiles (95th and 98th) aggregated at a 20 m grid resolution produced the strongest agreement with airborne lidar measurements (correlation coefficient (r) = 0.32–0.33, Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) = 7.57–9.05 m). When the comparison was limited to grid cells where PlanetScope and lidar heights differed by 7 m or less, agreement improved (r = 0.68–0.79, RMSE = 3.70–4.35 m). RF canopy height estimation models showed moderate accuracy across study sites (R 2 = 0.51–0.54, RMSE = 2.45–4.31 m). Multi-temporal analysis using generated 20 m canopy height maps revealed substantial canopy height reductions after wind disturbance, affecting 40.47% of Oakmulgee site, 36.52% of Flagg Mountain, and 60.92% of Weeks Bay. Overall, the approach provides a promising framework for assessing and monitoring forest disturbance impacts. It captures post-disturbance changes in forest structure with an ability to provide spatially explicit and timely information on canopy structure and thematic dynamics, particularly in areas where airborne lidar or field measurements are limited.

title: Revealing the influence of volcanic plumes on lake water quality parameters derived using remote sensing methods
summary: Satellite-derived observations of inland waters are widely used in environmental monitoring and climate research, often forming the basis of long-term analyses in the absence of continuous in situ measurements. However, the influence of transient atmospheric phenomena, such as volcanic plumes, on these datasets remains insufficiently quantified. In this study, we investigate the extent to which volcanic plumes influence lake surface water temperature (LSWT), turbidity, and chlorophyll-a measurements derived from ESA Climate Change Initiative (CCI) Lakes. Using a multi-sensor approach, we leverage MISR and MODIS observations to analyse plume–lake interactions during the 2011–2012 eruption of Puyehue-Cordón Caulle (PCC), Chile. Results indicate that while standard cloud screening procedures remove a substantial proportion of plume-affected observations, residual impacts remain. Notably, lake observations are influenced not only when plumes directly overlay the lake surface but also when plumes are proximal but not visually detectable over the lake, indicating the influence of diffuse aerosol particles. Analysis of aerosol microphysical properties demonstrates that particle-based classification can achieve approximately 67% accuracy, in identifying plume-affected observations but is limited by temporal variability in volcanic plume composition. In contrast, proximity-based approaches more consistently capture plume influence, suggesting that spatial context is critical for effective data flagging. These findings highlight a previously under-recognised source of uncertainty in satellite-derived inland water quality datasets. They support the implementation of proximity-based quality flags to improve data reliability in regions affected by volcanic activity in situations where consistent particle-based observations are unavailable.

title: A transferable satellite-derived bathymetry model without site-specific calibration for Case-1 optically shallow waters using Sentinel-2/MSI imagery
summary: Accurate bathymetry in optically shallow waters (OSWs), particularly across coral reef environments, is essential for coastal ecosystem management and benthic habitat monitoring. Satellite-derived bathymetry (SDB) offers a scalable alternative, but reliance on in situ depth measurements constrains its application in data-sparse OSW regions, while the coupling between water-column and benthic signals limits retrieval accuracy. Here, we developed OSW-SDB, a simulation-based SDB model for Case-1 OSWs that is not tailored to a specific region and accounts for variations in benthic reflectance. Using a newly developed benthic reflectance library comprising 2,100 spectra, we generated 200,000 pairs of water depth and remote sensing reflectance (Rrs) by radiative transfer simulations spanning diverse water-column optical properties and benthic reflectance conditions. An XGBoost model was trained based on the simulated dataset using SHAP-selected multispectral features, with 6,711 matched ICESat-2/ATL24 observations additionally used for hyperparameter optimization. OSW-SDB achieved coefficient of determination (R2) values above 0.96 and root mean square error (RMSE) values below 1 m on the simulated training and testing datasets. Two independent simulation-based validations using benthic spectra excluded from model development yielded R2 values of 0.84 and 0.94, and RMSEs of 2.26 and 1.35 m, respectively. Median absolute percentage errors (MdAPEs) were below 15% across all simulated datasets. This model was applied to Sentinel-2/MSI imagery after OSW extraction, producing spatially coherent 10-m bathymetry maps across seven OSW regions. Independent validation using 13,296 ATL24 depths covering 20 reef sites yielded an R2 of 0.80, an RMSE of 0.75 m, and an MdAPE of 26.13%. Additional evaluations using airborne LiDAR and in situ SeaBASS observations, together with comparisons against two existing SDB models, demonstrated stable performance across geographically diverse OSWs. The model is designed for Case-1 OSWs shallower than 20 m, with better performance below 10 m, consistent with the depth range of benthic habitat mapping. OSW-SDB enables practical and transferable bathymetric mapping at 10-m resolution across diverse Case-1 OSWs using only Sentinel-2/MSI imagery, without requiring site-specific bathymetric or benthic priors during application.
